title: Go Errors: Values, Wrapping, and Recovery
summary: A dense field guide to Go's error model — errors as ordinary values, sentinel and custom error types, wrapping with %w, inspection via errors.Is/As/Unwrap, and the separate world of panic, recover, and defer. Covers internals, idioms, performance trade-offs, and the mistakes that bite in production code.

chapters.title: Errors Are Values
points: `error` is a built-in interface, not a language construct: `type error interface { Error() string }`
Any type with an `Error() string` method satisfies `error` — no registration, no inheritance
Go has no exceptions for ordinary failure: functions return `(T, error)` as the last result
Idiom: `v, err := f(); if err != nil { return err }` — errors handled at the call site, not unwound
Zero value of `error` is `nil`; `nil` means success by convention, enforced only by discipline
Contract: when `err != nil`, other return values are undefined unless documented (e.g. `io.Reader` may return n>0 with err)
`errors.New("msg")` returns `*errorString`, a pointer — so two `errors.New` with same text are never `==`
`fmt.Errorf("read %s: %v", name, err)` formats a new error, flattening the cause into text
Error strings convention: lowercase, no trailing punctuation, no capitalisation — they get concatenated
Build context as a prefix chain: `openConfig: read /etc/app.conf: permission denied`
Errors are just data: they can be stored in slices, sent over channels, compared, and constructed at init time
`errors` package is tiny (New, Is, As, Unwrap, Join) — the power comes from the interface, not the package
Example: `var err error = myErr{}` — a non-pointer struct can implement error too
Comparison: Java/Python throw and unwind; Go returns and checks — control flow stays visible in the source

chapters.title: Creating and Returning Errors
points: `errors.New(text)` — cheapest error, allocates once, good for package-level sentinels
`fmt.Errorf(format, args...)` — formats and allocates; use for per-call contextual detail
Custom error type: `type PathError struct { Op, Path string; Err error }` with `func (e *PathError) Error() string`
Always implement `Error()` on the pointer receiver `*T` if the type is large or you compare identity
Custom types carry structured fields callers can read: status codes, offsets, retry hints
Constructor pattern: `func NewParseError(line int, err error) error { return &ParseError{Line: line, Err: err} }`
Add context at the boundary you cross, not at every frame — one wrap per layer, not per call
Never include the function name plus the caller's noun redundantly (`getUser: getUser failed`)
Stdlib examples: `*os.PathError`, `*net.OpError`, `*json.SyntaxError`, `*strconv.NumError`
`error` returned by value vs pointer: pointer types make identity comparison meaningful and cheap
Return `nil` explicitly on success; never return a zero-value custom struct as error
For errors that need no allocation, declare package-level `var ErrX = errors.New(...)` once at init
Example: `if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("load config %q: %w", path, err) }` — verb `%w` explained next chapter
Gotcha: `errors.New` inside a hot loop allocates each iteration; hoist it out

chapters.title: Sentinel Errors
points: Sentinel = exported package-level error value used as a signal: `var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")`
Naming convention: `Err` prefix for values, `Error` suffix for types (`ErrClosed` vs `SyntaxError`)
Classic sentinels: `io.EOF`, `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF`, `sql.ErrNoRows`, `os.ErrNotExist`, `context.Canceled`, `context.DeadlineExceeded`
`io.EOF` is not a failure — it is the normal termination signal for `Read`; treating it as an error is a bug
Compare with `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)`, not `err == ErrNotFound`, so wrapping still works
Sentinels become part of your public API: once callers compare against them you cannot change or remove them
Trade-off: sentinels couple caller to package but are the simplest possible signal
Prefer a behaviour check (`interface { Temporary() bool }`) or custom type when the error carries data
Anti-pattern: comparing error text with `strings.Contains(err.Error(), "not found")` — brittle, breaks on rewording
Sentinels can be typed: `type errNotFound struct{}` with a singleton var, giving both identity and type matching
Constant errors trick: `type errString string; func (e errString) Error() string { return string(e) }; const ErrX = errString("x")` — immutable, comparable
Sentinel must be a `var` when made by `errors.New` — you cannot make a `const` of pointer type
Gotcha: a caller can reassign your exported `var ErrX`; the const-error trick removes that hazard
Rule of thumb: export a sentinel only when callers must branch on that exact condition

chapters.title: Wrapping with %w and Unwrap
points: `fmt.Errorf` with `%w` produces a wrapping error that keeps a reference to the cause
`fmt.Errorf("query user %d: %w", id, err)` — text reads top-down, cause chain preserved bottom-up
`%w` vs `%v`: `%v` renders the cause as text and severs the chain; `%w` keeps it inspectable
The value returned by `%w` is an unexported `*fmt.wrapError` with fields `msg string` and `err error`
Unwrap contract: `func (e *T) Unwrap() error` returns the next error in the chain, or nil at the end
`errors.Unwrap(err)` calls that method once; it returns `nil` if the error does not implement `Unwrap`
Multiple `%w` in one `fmt.Errorf` (Go 1.20+) yields an error with `Unwrap() []error` — a tree, not a chain
`errors.Join(err1, err2, nil)` collects non-nil errors into one multi-error, skipping nils; returns nil if all nil
Joined errors format one per line; `Unwrap() []error` exposes them for `Is`/`As` traversal
Implementing `Unwrap` on a custom type: store `Err error` and return it — that is the whole contract
Wrapping is an API decision: exposing the cause lets callers depend on it, so wrap deliberately
To deliberately hide an implementation error, use `%v` — the chain stops and the internal type stays private
Example chain: `handler: service: repo: sql: no rows in result set` from three wraps over `sql.ErrNoRows`
Gotcha: `%w` on a nil error yields the literal text `%!w(<nil>)` — guard `err != nil` before wrapping
Pre-1.13 code used `github.com/pkg/errors` `Wrap`/`Cause`; `%w` + `errors.Is` is the stdlib replacement

chapters.title: errors.Is — Matching by Identity
points: `errors.Is(err, target)` reports whether any error in `err`'s chain matches `target`
Algorithm: compare `err == target`; if not, try `err.Is(target)`; then `errors.Unwrap` and repeat until nil
Comparability guard: `Is` only uses `==` when the target's type is comparable — otherwise it panics-free skips
For `Unwrap() []error`, `Is` walks the tree depth-first and returns true if any branch matches
`errors.Is(err, nil)` is true only when `err` itself is nil — not a useful check, use `err == nil`
Custom matching: implement `func (e *MyErr) Is(target error) bool` to declare equivalence to another value
Real example: `os.ErrNotExist` matches `*os.PathError` wrapping a syscall errno via a custom `Is` method
`errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)` is the correct timeout test — the raw value is often wrapped
`errors.Is(err, io.EOF)` after `io.Copy` or `bufio` calls that wrap the sentinel
Cost: `Is` is O(depth) pointer comparisons — trivial, safe inside handlers, avoid inside inner loops over millions of errors
Do not use `Is` to test types — that is `errors.As`'s job
Anti-pattern: `if err == sql.ErrNoRows` — breaks the moment any layer wraps with `%w`
Gotcha: a custom `Is` that always returns true makes every match succeed and silently swallows unrelated errors
Table row: `==` exact value only | `errors.Is` value anywhere in chain | `errors.As` type anywhere in chain

chapters.title: errors.As — Matching by Type
points: `errors.As(err, &target)` finds the first error in the chain assignable to `*target` and assigns it
Target must be a non-nil pointer to a type implementing `error`, or to an interface — else `As` panics
Usage: `var pe *os.PathError; if errors.As(err, &pe) { log(pe.Path) }` — access the structured fields
Returns `bool`; only when true is the target populated — never read the target after a false result
Walk order matches `Is`: check assignability, then `err.As(target)` if defined, then `Unwrap`, repeat
Custom hook: `func (e *MyErr) As(target any) bool` lets a type present itself as another type
Interface target: `var t interface{ Timeout() bool }; errors.As(err, &t)` — behaviour-based matching
Use `As` for errors that carry data (line numbers, HTTP status, offsets); use `Is` for pure signals
`As` uses reflection (`reflectlite`) for the assignability check — a few hundred ns, negligible outside hot loops
Panic cases to memorise: nil target, non-pointer target, pointer to a non-error non-interface type
Example: `var ne net.Error; if errors.As(err, &ne) && ne.Timeout() { retry() }`
Example: `var se *json.SyntaxError; errors.As(err, &se)` gives `se.Offset` for a parse position
Gotcha: passing the value rather than its address (`errors.As(err, pe)`) compiles but panics at run time
Gotcha: matching `*MyErr` when the code returned `MyErr` by value — the types differ, `As` returns false

chapters.title: Panic: Mechanics and Internals
points: `panic(v)` stops normal execution of the goroutine, runs deferred functions up the stack, then crashes the program
Panic value is `any`: usually an `error` or a string; `runtime.Error` for runtime-generated ones
Runtime panics: nil map write, nil pointer dereference, index out of range, slice bounds, integer divide by zero, type assertion failure, closed-channel send
Panic is per-goroutine but fatal for the process: an unrecovered panic in any goroutine kills everything
Unwinding runs each deferred call in LIFO order for every frame, printing the stack trace on exit with status 2
`GOTRACEBACK` env var controls trace verbosity: `none`, `single` (default), `all`, `system`, `crash`
Nested panic: panicking inside a deferred function during a panic prints both, labelled `panic: ... [recovered]`
`runtime.Goexit` also runs defers but terminates only the goroutine, with no panic value
Panic is for programmer errors and impossible states, never for expected failures like bad input or missing files
Stdlib panics rarely and loudly: `regexp.MustCompile`, `template.Must`, `sync.WaitGroup` misuse, `strconv` never
`Must*` convention: panic-on-error wrappers intended for package-level init where failure is unrecoverable
Cost: panic/recover is far more expensive than a return — stack walking, defer processing, no inlining
`fatal error:` (concurrent map writes, deadlock, out of memory) is NOT a panic and cannot be recovered
Example: `func mustEnv(k string) string { v, ok := os.LookupEnv(k); if !ok { panic("missing env "+k) }; return v }`

chapters.title: Defer and Recover
points: `recover()` stops a panic and returns its value — but only when called directly inside a deferred function
`recover()` outside a panic, or not directly deferred, returns `nil` and does nothing
Canonical form: `defer func() { if r := recover(); r != nil { err = fmt.Errorf("recovered: %v", r) } }()`
Converting panic to error requires a *named* return value — a bare `return` result cannot be reassigned
`defer` arguments evaluate immediately; the call itself runs at function exit — classic loop-variable trap
Defers run LIFO; each `defer` in a loop stacks up until the function returns, so avoid `defer` inside long loops
After `recover`, execution resumes in the *caller* of the panicking function, not at the panic site
Recover cannot cross goroutines: `go f()` panicking is not caught by the parent's recover
Every goroutine you spawn needs its own recover if a panic there must not kill the process
Legitimate uses: HTTP server middleware, plugin/user-code boundaries, recursive parsers using panic for control flow, test helpers
`net/http` recovers panics per request by default and closes the connection — but the handler's work is lost
Re-panic pattern: `if r := recover(); r != nil { if !isMine(r) { panic(r) } }` — only swallow your own signals
Never recover blindly: swallowing a nil-pointer panic leaves corrupted state running
Gotcha: `recover()` inside a helper called by the deferred function returns nil — it must be the deferred call itself
Debug trick: `debug.PrintStack()` or `debug.Stack()` inside recover, since the original trace is otherwise lost

chapters.title: Patterns, Pitfalls, and Trade-offs
points: The typed-nil trap: `var p *MyErr = nil; var e error = p; e != nil` is TRUE — interface has a type word
Fix: return `error` type variables, not concrete pointers; `if err != nil { return err }; return nil`
Never shadow: `if err := f(); err != nil` inside a block hides the outer `err` and can drop the failure
Do not log and return the same error — the caller logs it again, producing duplicate noise
Choose one boundary that logs (usually the top-level handler); everything below wraps and returns
Ignoring errors: `_ = f.Close()` is explicit and reviewable; a bare call is not — and `Close` on a writer can lose data
`defer f.Close()` on a *written* file swallows the flush error; capture it: `defer func(){ err = errors.Join(err, f.Close()) }()`
Error sets vs error trees: `errors.Join` for parallel failures (validation), `%w` chains for layered context
Retry decisions belong to behaviour, not identity: check `Timeout()`/`Temporary()`-style interfaces via `errors.As`
Comparison table row: sentinel = cheap, no data, tight coupling | custom type = data-rich, heavier API | opaque + behaviour = loosest coupling
Performance: `errors.New` and `fmt.Errorf` allocate; sentinel comparison does not; `As` costs reflection
Errors in concurrency: `errgroup.Group.Wait()` returns the first non-nil error and cancels the shared context
`context.Cause(ctx)` (Go 1.20+) returns the specific cancellation reason where `ctx.Err()` gives only Canceled/DeadlineExceeded
Testing: assert with `errors.Is`/`errors.As`, never on `err.Error()` strings; `t.Fatalf` on unexpected non-nil
Linters that catch these: `errcheck` (unchecked), `errorlint` (%v instead of %w, == on errors), `wrapcheck`

chapters.title: Summary and Decision Guide
points: Errors are values returned explicitly; panics are for bugs that make continuing meaningless
Decision: expected failure returns an error; impossible state panics; nothing in between
Create: `errors.New` for fixed text, `fmt.Errorf` for context, a struct type when callers need fields
Wrap with `%w` when the cause is part of your contract; use `%v` to deliberately keep it private
Inspect with `errors.Is` for a known value, `errors.As` for a known type, an interface assertion for behaviour
Never `==` an error and never match on `err.Error()` text
Implement `Unwrap() error` on wrapper types; `Unwrap() []error` for multi-errors; `Is`/`As` only for aliasing
`errors.Join` merges independent failures; the chain becomes a tree that `Is`/`As` still traverse
`recover` only in a directly deferred closure, only at a real boundary, with a named return to convert to error
Every `go` statement is a new panic domain — recover there or accept process death
Watch the typed-nil interface trap and error shadowing; both silently turn failures into successes
One layer, one wrap, one log site — context accumulates without duplication
Cheat sheet: `errors.New` | `fmt.Errorf(%w)` | `errors.Is` | `errors.As` | `errors.Unwrap` | `errors.Join` | `panic` | `recover` | `defer`
Version notes: `%w`/`Is`/`As`/`Unwrap` landed in Go 1.13; multi-`%w`, `errors.Join`, and `context.Cause` in Go 1.20
